passage:
"Dolma, you ate chips for breakfast?"
"Yogesh, mind your business."
"You said you were going to start running."
"I did. On Monday."
"It's Thursday."
Dolma threw a cushion at her brother. "I got tired. And bored. And my shoes hurt."
"So get new shoes. Or walk. You don't have to run like a crazy person."
"You're one to talk. You only play video games."
"Okay, deal. I'll walk with you if you eat real breakfast."
"Fine. Poha tomorrow. And you have to walk every day, not just when you feel like it."
"Every day?"
"Every day. Even if it's ten minutes."
The next morning they walked around the colony twice. Dolma complained the whole way, but she laughed more than she expected.

qa.q: What did Dolma eat for breakfast?
qa.a: She ate chips.

qa.q: Why did Dolma stop running after Monday?
qa.a: She felt tired, bored and her shoes hurt, so the plan she started with enthusiasm quickly felt too hard to keep up.

qa.q: What made the siblings' new plan more likely to last?
qa.a: They chose a smaller goal, walking even ten minutes every day, made a deal to keep each other going, and swapped chips for a real breakfast.

qa.q: How might Yogesh feel about walking every day?
qa.a: He may grumble, since he mostly plays video games, but joining his sister could make it fun for him too.

grounding: It shows siblings building consistent exercise and eating habits by making small, shared commitments.

passage: Last summer I decided to get fit, and I went at it like a crazy person. I'm Anirban. I ran every morning for an hour and skipped rice because some video said carbs were bad. By the second week my knees hurt, I was cranky, and I fell asleep in class. My friend Chinmay, who's on the football team, laughed at me, but kindly. He said his coach told them to build up slowly and eat properly, not cut whole foods. So I started again. Three short runs a week, stretching, rice and dal like normal. It felt too easy at first. But I didn't quit this time. Now, a year later, I run twice as far, and I still eat rice.

qa.q: How many short runs a week did Anirban start with the second time?
qa.a: He started with three short runs a week.

qa.q: How did Anirban feel after his first two weeks?
qa.a: He was in pain, cranky and exhausted, which shows the extreme plan was hurting rather than helping him.

qa.q: Why did Anirban's second approach work better?
qa.a: Building up slowly and eating normally was sustainable, so he didn't burn out and kept going for a year.

qa.q: How might Chinmay feel seeing Anirban's progress a year later?
qa.a: He'd probably feel pleased that his coach's advice helped and proud of his friend's consistency. 👍

grounding: A teen reflects on replacing an extreme fitness plan with a consistent, balanced routine.

passage:
PE teacher's note, Class 9:
Thomas has been skipping PE for three weeks, saying he forgot his kit. His classmate Karthik mentioned Thomas said he's "bad at sports" and doesn't want to be laughed at. I spoke to Thomas privately. He admitted he gets out of breath fast and felt embarrassed. I explained fitness is built slowly and that everyone starts somewhere. We agreed he'd try skipping rope, which he enjoys, for a few minutes each lesson, building up weekly. I also talked about drinking water, sleep and eating proper meals, not just snacks. I asked Karthik to partner with him.
Follow-up: Thomas has come to four lessons in a row. He still gets out of breath, but he's smiling more.

qa.q: What activity did Thomas agree to try?
qa.a: He agreed to try skipping rope.

qa.q: Why was Thomas skipping PE?
qa.a: He felt embarrassed about getting out of breath and feared being laughed at, so he used forgotten kit as an excuse.

qa.q: What made the teacher's plan work for Thomas?
qa.a: He spoke privately, chose an activity Thomas enjoys, built it up slowly, and paired him with Karthik for support.

qa.q: How might Karthik feel being asked to partner with Thomas?
qa.a: He might feel trusted and glad to help, since he already noticed Thomas was struggling.

grounding: A PE teacher's note shows helping a teen build a consistent fitness habit and healthy eating.

passage:
Monday. Day 18!
Skipping rope on the terrace before school: done. It's harder when it's cold and my legs want to stay in bed, but I've marked every day on the calendar and I don't want a gap. Saurabh bhaiya tried it with me today and gave up after two minutes. 'Sonali, how?' HA.
What's changed: I'm less out of breath on the stairs. I eat breakfast now, poha or eggs, instead of skipping it. And I wash my face after every workout because sweat plus my oily skin was giving me spots.
What's not changed: I still want samosas. I had one on Saturday and didn't feel guilty. Mumma says that's the right attitude.
Goal: keep going through exams, even if it's just ten minutes.

qa.q: What exercise does Sonali do on the terrace?
qa.a: Skipping rope, before school.

qa.q: How does Sonali seem to feel about the calendar streak?
qa.a: Sonali feels proud and motivated, not wanting to leave a gap even on hard mornings.

qa.q: What makes Sonali's habits likely to last?
qa.a: Sonali is consistent but flexible, eats breakfast, looks after skin and doesn't feel guilty about a samosa.

qa.q: What might Saurabh think after giving up after two minutes?
qa.a: He might be surprised at how fit Sonali has become and a bit impressed.

grounding: A teen records building a consistent exercise, eating and skin-care routine.

passage: Every morning at half past five, Chetan's alarm was the rooster next door. In the first week of the monsoon holidays he ran to the canal bridge and back, then gave up on the fourth day when the mud swallowed his chappal. His elder sister Sarita, home from nursing college, watched him eat three packets of chips on the verandah that afternoon. "District kabaddi trials are in two months," she said. "You want to run hard once, or a little every day?" She drew a calendar on the back of a wedding card: a short run, skipping in the yard if it rained, and a tick for every meal with dal, curd or eggs. Chetan grumbled. But the ticks started adding up. By the third week he woke before the rooster, and the chips stayed in the shop.

qa.q: What did Sarita draw the calendar on?
qa.a: The back of a wedding card.

qa.q: Why did Chetan grumble about the calendar?
qa.a: Chetan felt a bit annoyed and embarrassed at being organised by his sister after giving up, though the ticks quietly motivated him.

qa.q: What made Sarita's plan easier to keep than Chetan's first attempt?
qa.a: It had a rainy-day option and small daily ticks, so one muddy day didn't end the whole routine.

qa.q: How might Sarita feel seeing the chips stay in the shop by the third week?
qa.a: Sarita would probably feel pleased and proud that a simple, steady plan stuck instead of a burst of effort that fizzled.

grounding: A village teenager builds steady exercise and eating habits with his sister's simple daily plan.

passage: Felix used to eat a petrol-station pastry on the way to football practice in Leipzig, then wonder why his legs felt like wet socks by the second half. Abebe, the team's fastest winger, always had the same brown paper bag: a cheese sandwich, an apple, a bottle of tap water. "Boring," Felix said. "Boring works," Abebe said. "My mum says: same thing, every day, no drama." In January Felix tried it, grudgingly. He packed the night before, set the bag by the door, and added ten minutes of skipping in the courtyard before school. On rainy mornings he skipped under the stairwell. By March he hadn't magically become fast. But he stopped fading in the second half, and he noticed he felt cross on the days he forgot the bag.

qa.q: What was in Abebe's brown paper bag?
qa.a: A cheese sandwich, an apple and a bottle of tap water.

qa.q: What does Felix feeling cross on forgotten-bag days suggest?
qa.a: Felix now feels uneasy without the routine, a sign it has become a habit he values rather than a chore.

qa.q: What made the new routine stick for Felix?
qa.a: Packing the night before and having a rainy-day spot for skipping removed daily decisions, so the habit stayed consistent.

qa.q: How might Abebe see Felix's change by March?
qa.a: Abebe would probably feel quietly amused and pleased that 'boring works' turned out to be true for a teammate too.

grounding: A German teenager copies a teammate's plain, consistent food and exercise routine and sees it last.

passage: At the athletics hostel in Ranchi, the breakfast bell rang at 6:45, and most days Jyoti slept through it. She grabbed a biscuit packet on the way to the track, and by the fourth lap her legs felt like sandbags. Coach Ekka noticed her slowing and waved her to the bench. "What did you eat?" "Biscuits." "That's not fuel. And you're on your phone till midnight, aren't you?" Jyoti looked down at her spikes. Her roommate Bidisha, who never missed breakfast, offered a deal: phones in the locker at ten, and she would shake Jyoti awake for the bell. The first week was miserable. By the second, Jyoti was eating poha and a banana before training and finishing her laps strong. She wrote "10 pm" on the mirror in eyeliner so she wouldn't forget.

qa.q: What time did the breakfast bell ring?
What does Jyoti looking down at her spikes suggest?
qa.a: Jyoti seems embarrassed and a bit guilty, knowing the coach is right about the late nights and biscuit breakfasts.

qa.q: Which part of the deal made the change last?
qa.a: Locking phones away at ten fixed the real cause, late nights, and Bidisha's wake-up made breakfast easy to reach; the mirror note kept it going.

qa.q: What is it like for Bidisha to take on the wake-up job?
qa.a: Bidisha probably finds it a small effort worth making, and may feel glad to see her roommate running strongly.

grounding: At a sports hostel, a teenager fixes her sleep and breakfast habits with a roommate's help.

passage:
Dear Raghav,
You asked how I started running. Here's the truth.
In January, I couldn't run to the end of our lane without stopping. I felt embarrassed because my younger cousin beat me.
So I made a plan: three mornings a week, run one minute, walk one minute, for twenty minutes. I wrote each day in a notebook with a tick.
Some mornings it was cold and I stayed in bed. But I didn't break the chain twice in a row.
I also started eating proper breakfast: eggs or poha, fruit. And I bathe right after running, because I got a rash once from sweaty clothes.
It's April. Yesterday I ran the whole twenty minutes without stopping.
Try it with me? We can tick our notebooks together.
Vijay

qa.q: How many mornings a week did Vijay run?
qa.a: Three mornings a week.

qa.q: What was Vijay feeling on being beaten by a younger cousin?
qa.a: Vijay felt embarrassed about Vijay's own fitness.

qa.q: What habits helped Vijay stay consistent?
qa.a: A simple run-walk plan, ticking a notebook, not missing twice in a row, and eating proper breakfast.

qa.q: How might Raghav feel reading this?
qa.a: Raghav might feel encouraged to start, since Vijay offers to do it together.

grounding: A teen writes to a cousin about building a consistent running and eating routine.

passage:
My coach Pradeep Sir used to say, "Talent shows up once. Habits show up every day." I didn't get it at first.
I'm Anirban. In Class 9, I was on the football team but always tired by the second half. I ate chips before practice and skipped breakfast.
Pradeep Sir sat me down. "What did you eat today?" I told him. He just raised his eyebrows.
So I changed small things. Breakfast every day. A banana before practice, not chips. Water bottle always with me. Two extra fitness sessions a week.
The first month was boring. No big change. By the third month, I was running as hard in the last minute as the first.
That's when I understood what he meant. It wasn't magic. It was just every day.

qa.q: What did Anirban eat before practice at first?
qa.a: Chips.

qa.q: What was Anirban feeling when Pradeep Sir raised his eyebrows?
qa.a: Anirban felt a bit embarrassed about the chips and skipped breakfast.

qa.q: What choice inside the story made the difference?
qa.a: Deciding to change small daily habits and sticking with them even when the first month felt boring.

qa.q: How might Pradeep Sir have felt seeing Anirban in the third month?
qa.a: Pradeep Sir probably felt proud that Anirban finally understood his saying.

grounding: A young person tells how Anirban built consistent fitness and eating habits with a coach's guidance.

passage:
I'm Jatin, Tejas's cousin. Tejas used to be really upset about his skin; he had spots all over his forehead and would hide under a cap.
This year I noticed a routine. Every morning at six, he skips rope in the courtyard for fifteen minutes. Then he washes his face with a mild soap, not scrubbing hard. He carries a small towel to wipe sweat after games.
He also stopped drinking three colas a day. Now it's water or lassi.
His skin isn't perfect. But he doesn't wear the cap all the time now. And he beat me in a race last week.
I asked how he stuck with it. He shrugged. "I just do it every day."

qa.q: How long does Tejas skip rope every morning?
qa.a: Fifteen minutes.

qa.q: What might Tejas have been feeling when he hid under a cap?
qa.a: Tejas was probably self-conscious and unhappy about his skin.

qa.q: What parts of Tejas's routine could others copy?
qa.a: Short daily exercise, gentle face washing, wiping sweat after games, and swapping colas for water or lassi.

qa.q: How does Jatin see Tejas's change?
qa.a: Jatin notices the steady routine and new confidence and is impressed, especially after losing the race.

grounding: A cousin watches a teen build a consistent fitness and skin-care routine.

passage:
Week 1: Anjali decided to start running with her brother Karthik before school. Five minutes in, she was gasping and walked home. Karthik didn't laugh, just said, "Tomorrow, same time."
Week 3: She'd kept going, but slowly: run one minute, walk one minute, for twenty minutes. Some mornings she hated it. She also noticed she was starving afterwards and started eating a proper breakfast, eggs and a banana, instead of skipping it for the bus.
Week 6: On a cool Sunday, she ran the whole park loop without stopping. Karthik was behind her, for once.
She didn't feel like an athlete. But she felt steadier in class, and she was sleeping better. She pinned a calendar to her wall and put a tick on every running day.

qa.q: What did Anjali start eating for breakfast?
qa.a: Eggs and a banana.

qa.q: How did Anjali feel after running the whole park loop?
qa.a: Anjali felt steadier and quietly proud, even if she didn't feel like an athlete.

qa.q: Which habit helped most, and why?
qa.a: Running little and often with walking breaks helped, because it was manageable enough to keep up for weeks.

qa.q: How might Karthik feel seeing her ahead of him in week 6?
qa.a: Karthik probably feels proud of his sister and pleased that his patience helped her keep going.

grounding: Illustrates a teen building a consistent fitness and eating habit over several weeks.

passage:
Pallavi, you want to train two hours every day from tomorrow? I did that once. Listen.
I was fifteen, Sahil the skinny one. A new gym opened near our house. I decided to become strong in a month. First week, I lifted every day, skipped rest, ate only eggs. By day nine my shoulder hurt so badly I couldn't lift my school bag. The doctor said to rest, and I sat out for three weeks, angry and sulking.
My coach at the time said, "Strong is built like a wall. One brick a day, not all at once."
So I started again, slowly. Three days a week. Dal, rice, vegetables, not just eggs. Sleep. It took a year. But I never stopped again.
That's why your Sahil Mama will make you start with twenty minutes.

qa.q: What happened to young Sahil's shoulder by day nine?
qa.a: It hurt so badly that young Sahil couldn't lift the school bag.

qa.q: How did young Sahil feel sitting out for three weeks?
qa.a: Young Sahil felt angry and frustrated, sulking about the lost time.

qa.q: What was the turning point in Sahil's story, and why?
qa.a: Starting again slowly, three days a week with balanced meals, because steady habits lasted where rushing had failed.

qa.q: How might the coach have felt watching young Sahil come back?
qa.a: The coach was probably relieved and pleased that the boy had learned patience rather than quitting.

grounding: Shows an elder recounting how rushed training failed and consistent fitness and eating habits worked.

passage:
Yusuf had played football every evening until his Class 12 boards started. Now there was no time, the family's flat was one room and a kitchen, and the park was far.
He felt sluggish and snappish. His mother, Sangeeta, noticed him snacking on chips at midnight.
"You used to be happy after football," she said.
"No time, Ammi. No space."
They worked it out together. Fifteen minutes every morning before study: skipping rope on the roof, push-ups and squats beside the bed. Water bottle on the desk. Fruit instead of chips for the late-night hunger, and dinner a little later so he wasn't starving.
The first week he missed three days. The second, only one. By the end of the month, he wasn't as snappish, and his notes looked tidier. "Fifteen minutes is nothing," he said. "But it's not nothing."

qa.q: What did Yusuf do on the roof each morning?
qa.a: He did skipping rope.

qa.q: How did Yusuf feel before the new routine?
qa.a: Yusuf felt sluggish and snappish, missing the football that used to make him happy.

qa.q: What made the plan work despite little time and space?
qa.a: Keeping it short and at the same time daily, using the roof and bedside, and swapping chips for fruit made it easy to stick to.

qa.q: How might Sangeeta feel by the end of the month?
qa.a: Sangeeta probably feels relieved and pleased to see her son calmer and more focused.

grounding: Illustrates a teen keeping a consistent fitness and eating routine under exam-time and space constraints.

passage: Farida's alarm went off at 6:10, and for the third morning in a row she wanted to switch it off. Two weeks ago she had started running laps in the colony park with her neighbour Siddharth, who was training for the school relay. The first day she had tried to keep up with him and ended up bent over near the swings, gasping. Now she ran at her own pace, walked when she needed to, and ticked off mornings on a calendar taped to her cupboard. Her mother had started keeping boiled chana and a banana on the counter, so Farida stopped grabbing chips on the way to the bus. This morning a drizzle was falling. Siddharth texted, "Still on? 🙂" She laced her shoes, grumbling under her breath, and went.

qa.q: Where did Farida run with Siddharth?
qa.a: She ran laps in the colony park.

qa.q: What was Farida feeling when her alarm rang, and what made her go anyway?
qa.a: She felt reluctant and sleepy, but the ticked-off calendar and Siddharth's text helped her feel committed enough to go.

qa.q: What went wrong on the first day, and what fixed it?
qa.a: She tried to match a relay runner and ended up gasping; running at her own pace and walking when needed made the habit one she could keep.

qa.q: How might Farida's mother see her part in the new routine?
qa.a: She is likely quietly pleased that keeping easy food on the counter helps Farida eat better without any nagging.

grounding: Shows a teen building a consistent exercise and eating routine through small, repeatable steps.
